title: Your Customer Is Your Next Competitor: The Rise of Customer-Built Software (2026)
summary: Build vs buy software in 2026: AI lets customers build their own CRMs, client portals, and internal tools. See when building beats buying SaaS, and why.
body_markdown:
Every SaaS founder should spend a day watching their customers work.


Watch the sales manager export leads to a spreadsheet because the CRM doesn't quite fit. Watch the account manager copy customer information between tools. Watch the operations team maintain a dashboard nobody has time to update.


These aren't edge cases. They're the little workarounds that accumulate when software doesn't match how a business actually runs.


For years, customers accepted them. Changing software was expensive. Custom development was even more expensive. And the people who understood the problem rarely had the technical skills to solve it.


AI is changing that equation. The next competitor to a SaaS company might be the customer who knows exactly what the product is missing.


> **TL;DR:** Build vs buy software now has a new answer: describe it. The people closest to the work can build the CRM, portal, or dashboard they need. In a census of 471 top-traffic paid Taskade Genesis apps, dashboards led at 28.2% of traffic. Rent the systems of record. Build the rest.[Build your first app →](https://www.taskade.com/create?entry_kind=content&source=blog&entry=%2Fblog%2Fbuild-vs-buy-software)


The CRM below is a real Taskade Genesis app kit, not a mockup. Click around in it. It runs on a workspace with 2 projects, 1 AI agent and 2 automations, and you can[clone the Neon CRM Dashboard kit](https://www.taskade.com/apps/featured/neon-crm-dashboard-nsrm12wns3e1cgni) into your own workspace and change it. Cloning it needs a paid plan, because the kit includes automations.

## 🧭 Build vs Buy Software in 2026: The Short Answer


The short answer to build vs buy software in 2026: buy the systems of record, build the operational tools that make your business different. AI app builders now let the person who runs a workflow describe the tool and get a working app, so "build" no longer means "hire developers".


Most build vs buy guides are written for an enterprise IT buyer with a budget and a development team. This one is written for two other people: the business owner who can now build a CRM or a client portal without code, and the SaaS founder whose customer just did.


Question Short answer


What should I still buy? Payroll, the accounting ledger, payments, email delivery at scale, and anything a regulator or auditor checks


What can I build now? CRMs, client portals, operations dashboards, intake systems, invoice trackers and other tools shaped like your process


Who builds it? The person who runs the workflow, by describing it in plain English


What does building cost? A plan, your time, and the upkeep: testing, permissions, data quality and support


What is the common middle path? Keep the system of record and build the missing piece next to it


What should a SaaS founder do? Make the product easy to build on, so customer-built tools connect to it instead of replacing it


Four questions decide most cases. Is the workflow your edge? Does a regulator check it? How many seats would you pay for to use a small part of the product? Who changes the tool when the process changes?


The rest of this post explains why the answer changed, what people actually build, and how to make the call for your own business.


---


## 👀 The People Closest to the Work


The people who understand a business process best are the people who run it every day, not the people who write its software. That gap between knowing a problem and building its fix is what AI app builders are starting to close.


Think about who actually understands a business process. The sales manager knows why a deal keeps getting stuck. The account manager knows what every client asks for. The operations manager knows which spreadsheet absolutely cannot break.


That knowledge usually lives outside the software. It lives in people's heads, spreadsheets, emails, documents, and years of experience.


Who knows the work What they know that the software does not Where that knowledge lives today The workaround you will find


Sales manager Why a deal stalls, and which signals mean a lead is real Notes, call memory, a private spreadsheet Leads exported weekly to a sheet with extra columns


Account manager What each client asks for, and when Email threads and a shared doc Client details copied between three tools


Operations manager Which numbers matter on Monday morning A dashboard spreadsheet with manual updates A report rebuilt by hand every week


Office manager How a request moves from intake to done Inbox folders and sticky notes A form, a sheet and a reminder email, glued together


Founder Which exceptions the business cannot afford Their own head "Ask me first" as the approval process


Traditional software development starts with requirements. Someone explains the business to a product manager. The product manager writes specifications. Designers turn those into interfaces. Developers build the application. Everyone hopes the original problem survived the translation.


Sometimes it does. Often, something gets lost.


Now imagine the person doing the work can describe what they need and get a working application. The distance between understanding a problem and building its solution gets much shorter.


That's a bigger change than faster coding. It's a change in who gets to build.


---


## 🧾 Why Businesses Have Lived With Software That Almost Works


Businesses live with software that almost works because packaged SaaS must serve thousands of customers at once, and the alternative, custom development, cost far more. The result is a stack of subscriptions plus a layer of spreadsheets that fill the gaps.


SaaS made sophisticated software accessible without having to build it yourself. That was an enormous improvement over buying servers, installing applications, and maintaining custom systems.


But packaged software comes with a tradeoff: it has to work for many customers.


Your CRM has someone else's pipeline assumptions. Your client portal has someone else's account structure. Your dashboard measures what the vendor decided to include.


Businesses adapt. They add spreadsheets. They subscribe to another tool. They hire contractors to connect the systems. They train employees to work around missing features.


Eventually, the workarounds become part of the business. Here is what that looks like in practice, next to the same process as a built app:


```text
BEFORE: the spreadsheet workaround          AFTER: one built app on one workspace
───────────────────────────────────         ─────────────────────────────────────
CRM (rented)                                Pipeline app (built)
│  export leads every Friday                │  leads arrive from the intake form
▼                                           ▼
leads.xlsx  + 6 extra columns               Projects: one record per lead,
│  "Status (REAL)", "Owner?",               │  with the fields your team uses
│  "Last call", "Notes v2"                  ▼
▼                                         AI agent: drafts a qualification
Email to the team: "use v3"                   │  note on each new lead
│                                           ▼
▼                                         Automation: when a deal moves
Manager rebuilds the report                   │  stage, assign it and send
│  by hand on Monday                        │  the follow-up email
▼                                           ▼
Two versions of the truth                   One version of the truth,
by Wednesday                                  visible to the whole team


```


Consider two hypothetical companies. One pays $500 a month for software that primarily manages records and user access. Another spends $20,000 developing a tailored application.


Those numbers aren't universal market averages. They illustrate the economic decision businesses face. For a long time, the choice was to buy something close enough or pay substantially more to build something tailored.


Now there's a third option. Describe the system you need and build it yourself.


The honest comparison is total cost of ownership, not the sticker price. A subscription bundles hosting, security, support and updates into one line item. A built tool moves part of that work to you: maintenance, security, data quality and support for the people who use it.


Cost line (illustrative) Rent generic SaaS Commission custom software Build it yourself on an AI workspace


Upfront cost Low: a subscription starts today High: the illustrative $20,000 build Low: a plan plus your own time


Ongoing cost The illustrative $500 a month, rising with seats Hosting, fixes and developer hours The plan, plus the hours you spend on upkeep

Who maintains it The vendor Your developer or agency You and your team

## 📜 Your Spreadsheet Is Already Custom Software


Every business that runs on a spreadsheet next to its SaaS already builds its own software. The spreadsheet is the custom tool. It is only a fragile one, with no permissions, no automation and no single version of the truth.


Retool, which sells a platform for internal tools, found in its 2020 State of Internal Tools survey that more than 40% of 310 respondents used Google Sheets to build internal tools ([Retool, 2020](https://retool.com/blog/state-of-internal-tools-2020) ). In its 2022 survey, technical teams spent 33% of their time on internal tools ([Retool, 2022](https://retool.com/blog/state-of-internal-tools-2022) ).


Research on spreadsheet accuracy explains why that matters. Ray Panko collected nine development experiments in which people built spreadsheets alone, and their average cell error rates ran from 1.1% to 5.6% ([Panko, Spreadsheet Development Experiments](https://panko.com/ssr/DevelopmentExperiments.html) ). Real companies fare no better. Nine field audits with known methods examined 163 operational spreadsheets and found errors in 84% of them ([Panko, Audits of Operational Spreadsheets](https://panko.com/ssr/Audits.html) ). Even a small error rate per cell adds up to a likely mistake in a large sheet, which anyone who has found a broken formula in a report already knows.


Business teams also build outside IT more each year:


Signal Figure Source


Employees who acquire, modify or create technology outside IT's visibility 41% in 2022, forecast 75% by 2027[Gartner](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2023-03-28-gartner-unveils-top-8-cybersecurity-predictions-for-2023-2024) , Mar 28, 2023


Technology solutions developed outside centralized IT 15.3%[Gartner, CIO Planning for 2027](https://www.gartner.com/en/articles/cio-planning-for-2027) , 2026


Tech executives who expect AI to expand business-developed solutions by 2030 80%[Gartner, CIO Planning for 2027](https://www.gartner.com/en/articles/cio-planning-for-2027) , 2026


So the question for most owners is not whether to build custom software. You already do. The question is whether your custom software stays a spreadsheet or becomes an app with records, permissions and automation behind it.

## 🛠️ The Customer Becomes the Builder


The customer becomes the builder when the person who owns a workflow can turn it into software directly. AI app builders let a business operator describe a process in plain English, get a working application, and keep adjusting it without a development team.


Your next CRM could be built by your sales manager. Your next client portal by your account manager. Your next operations dashboard by the person running operations.


These people already understand the requirements. They know the exceptions, the approval steps, the records that matter, and the things that go wrong on a Friday afternoon.


What they haven't had is a practical way to turn that knowledge into software.


AI app builders are starting to close that gap. A business operator can describe a workflow in plain English and generate an application to support it. They can inspect the result, adjust it, and connect the relevant data and processes. If you have never written code, the comparison of[free AI app builders](https://www.taskade.com/blog/free-ai-app-builders) helps you pick a tool.


The result doesn't have to replace a company's entire software stack. It might replace one spreadsheet. One manual process. One expensive add-on. One internal tool that never made it onto the engineering roadmap. These small, single-purpose tools have a name, micro apps, and they are where most customer-built software starts.


That's where the change begins. A 2026 survey from Retool, of 817 of its customers and builders, puts numbers on it ([Retool 2026 Build vs. Buy report](https://retool.com/blog/ai-build-vs-buy-report-2026) , Feb 17, 2026):


Finding from Retool's 2026 survey Figure


Teams that replaced at least one SaaS tool with a custom build 35%


Builders who plan to build more custom tools in 2026 78%


Builders whose team uses production software built with AI 51%, and 49% of those save 6+ hours a week


Builders who built something outside IT oversight in the past year 60%


Their top reasons Speed 31%, unmet needs 25%, slow IT process 18%


Retool's respondents are its own users, so the sample leans toward people who already build. The direction still matches what Gartner reports from the IT side. Retool also names the risk in the same report: "Time saved on one task can be offset by time lost to maintenance, wrangling ungoverned tool sprawl, or triaging security vulnerabilities." Keep that sentence in mind for the scorecard below.

## 🔀 Build, Buy, Extend or Describe: The Four Options


Most build vs buy guides list three options: build custom software, buy a product, or buy a product and extend it. AI adds a fourth: describe the tool and run it on a workspace. Each option differs in who changes the software, how the cost grows and who owns the upkeep.


Build (custom code) Buy (SaaS) Buy and extend Describe (AI workspace)


Time to first version Weeks to months Days Days, then weeks for the extension Minutes to hours


Who changes it Developers The vendor The vendor, plus your developer or a consultant The person who runs the workflow


Cost shape Large upfront, then hosting and developer hours Per seat, every month Per seat, plus integration work A plan, plus your upkeep time


Data ownership Yours, in your database In the vendor's product, with export Split across the product and the extension In your workspace, with export


Maintenance owner Your developer or agency The vendor Both, which is where gaps appear You and your team, on hosted infrastructure


The describe option is not free of work. It moves the build work to minutes and leaves the ownership work with you. That trade suits the tools that change often and that only your team uses. It suits less well the tools where a mistake costs money or a compliance finding.

## 📊 What Are People Actually Building?


People who build their own software mostly build operational tools, not landing pages. In a first-party analysis of 471 top-traffic paid Taskade Genesis apps, the largest category was dashboards and analytics, at 28.2% of traffic, across 151 apps.


At Taskade, we've seen this behavior in our own product. Across those 471 applications were 2,778 connected projects and 1,078 AI agents.

Next categories Calculators and tools 12.9%, booking and scheduling 10.0%, education 7.7%


Connected projects 2,778


AI agents 1,078

These aren't simply landing pages. People are building operational tools: dashboards, trackers, client portals, CRMs, booking systems, and applications that help manage everyday work.


The data is limited to this specific cohort, not the software market as a whole. But it tells us something useful about what people want when building becomes easier. They often start with the work they're already doing.


Retool's survey points the same way from a different sample. Workflow automations led the categories its respondents replaced or considered replacing, at 35%. Internal admin software followed at 33%, BI software at 29%, CRMs and form builders at 25%, and project management software at 23%.

## 🧬 An App Is Only the Beginning


An app is only the beginning because a business tool must remember records, act on them and keep running after the first build. Taskade Genesis connects each app to a Taskade workspace, so the screen sits on top of projects, AI agents and automations that do the work.


Generating a screen is becoming easier. Running a business on that screen is a different challenge.


A CRM needs customer records, pipeline state, permissions, and follow-ups. A client portal needs the right information for the right customer. An operations dashboard needs data that changes as work gets done.


Software has to remember what happened yesterday, execute what needs to happen today, and make tomorrow's work easier.


That's the idea behind Taskade Genesis. Instead of generating an isolated interface, Taskade Genesis connects an app to the surrounding Taskade workspace.


- **Projects** hold structured business information and shared context.
- **AI agents** help process information, reason, and carry out supported tasks.
- **Automations** connect triggers and actions across recurring workflows.
- **Apps** give people an interface for working with the system.


Projects remember. Agents reason. Automations run. Apps serve.


The app is the surface. The workspace is the runtime. The architecture post,[Software That Runs Itself](https://www.taskade.com/blog/software-runs-itself) , explains how the four layers share one runtime.

Automations (execution) Run steps when something happens Assign a deal and send a follow-up when it moves stage Send a confirmation when a client submits a form

## 🧮 The Owner's Scorecard


The owner's scorecard turns the build vs buy decision into one number. Score a tool from 1 to 5 on seven criteria, multiply each score by its weight, and add the results. A high total favors building, a low total favors buying, and the middle favors keeping the product and building next to it.


Score each criterion for how strongly it favors building. A 5 means "this points hard toward building". A 1 means "this points hard toward buying".


Criterion Weight Scores 5 (build) when Scores 1 (buy) when


Fit to your process 20% No product matches how you work A product matches it out of the box


Workaround hours each week 20% The team loses hours to copy-paste and spreadsheets There is no workaround today


Rental cost over 3 years 15% Many seats pay for a small part of a product The subscription is small and fully used


Cost of a failure 15% A mistake is cheap and quick to fix A mistake costs money, safety or a compliance finding


Data sensitivity 10% Internal, non-regulated data Regulated, financial or health data


How often the process changes 10% Every month or quarter Rarely


Who can own upkeep 10% A named person has time for it Nobody does


Read the weighted total like this: above 3.5, build it. Between 2.5 and 3.5, keep the product and build the missing piece next to it. Below 2.5, keep buying.

## ⚖️ Should Every Company Build Its Own Software?


No company should build all of its own software. Buying still wins for accounting, regulated workflows and security-sensitive systems. Building wins for smaller operational tools where your process is unique, the workaround costs hours every week, and you only use a fraction of a paid product.


Of course not. Buying established software still makes sense for complex accounting, regulated workflows, security-sensitive systems, and applications where mature integrations, ongoing support, and proven reliability outweigh customization.


Software doesn't become free to operate just because it becomes cheaper to generate. Someone still has to consider security, permissions, data quality, reliability, maintenance, and what happens when things go wrong.


But the calculation is changing for smaller operational tools. If your company has a unique workflow, if existing software requires constant workarounds, or if a relatively simple internal application would save hours every week, building something tailored deserves serious consideration.


The decision becomes less about whether you can afford a development team and more about whether the software delivers enough value to justify building and maintaining it.


### What you should still buy


Some software is worth renting for as long as your business exists, because the vendor carries legal, financial or deliverability risk that a small team cannot.


Keep buying Why What you can build next to it


Payroll Tax tables, filings and penalties change every year A time-off request app that feeds the payroll system


Accounting ledger Your accountant and auditors work in it An invoice tracker tied to the work delivered


Payments processing Card security and fraud rules A client portal that links to the payment page


Email delivery at scale Sender reputation and spam rules An intake system that sends through your email provider


Systems that hold regulated data Audits, certifications and breach rules A non-sensitive scheduling or status app


Notice the third column. The most common answer is not "replace the product". It is "build the missing piece next to it". A business keeps its accounting system and builds the invoice tracker. It keeps its email platform and builds the intake system that feeds it. With 100+ integrations, a built tool can read from and write to the systems you keep renting.


Before you build, write down who owns the tool. A built app needs the same care as any system the business depends on: permissions set with role-based access from Owner to Viewer, a test with real data, and a person who answers when something looks wrong.

## 🏢 What Happens to SaaS?


SaaS is not disappearing, but its advantages are shifting. A long feature list and a generic interface defend a product less when customers can build what they need. Reliability, proprietary data, distribution and deep expertise defend it more.


SaaS isn't disappearing. Great software companies do far more than produce code. They maintain infrastructure, protect customer data, integrate complex systems, support users, and continually improve their products. Those responsibilities remain valuable.


But some familiar advantages are getting weaker. A long feature list is less convincing when customers can create tailored functionality. A generic interface is less defensible when alternatives become easier to build. A high subscription price is harder to justify when customers only need a fraction of the product.


Meanwhile, the things that are difficult to reproduce become more important: reliability, distribution, customer relationships, proprietary data, deep expertise, and the ability to deliver results consistently.


Advantage Weaker when customers can build Stronger when customers can build


Long feature list Yes: customers build the features they need


Generic, one-size interface Yes: a tailored screen is a prompt away


Per-seat price for a fraction of the product Yes: the math invites a build


Reliability and uptime record Yes: hard to reproduce in a weekend


Proprietary data and network effects Yes: a built tool cannot copy them


Compliance, security and audits Yes: the vendor carries the risk


Distribution and customer relationships Yes: trust compounds over years


Deep domain expertise Yes: it shapes defaults customers keep


The opportunity for SaaS companies is to understand their customers better and make products worth continuing to pay for. The opportunity for customers is to stop waiting for every feature request.

## 🧑‍💼 For SaaS Founders: When Your Customer Becomes Your Competitor


A SaaS founder loses a customer to a custom build one workaround at a time. The customer adds a spreadsheet, then builds one missing piece, then moves the workflow into it, and the seat count falls. The defense is to make your product the platform those tools build on.


Customers rarely cancel in one step. The path usually looks like this:


For a SaaS founder, the practical response starts with the day spent watching customers work. Every spreadsheet next to your product is a feature request your customer is building without you. You can treat it as a threat, or you can make your product the system of record those custom tools connect to.


Defense What it means in practice Why it keeps the customer


A public API Customers can read and write their data from their own tools A built tool connects to you instead of replacing you


Webhooks Your product tells other tools when something changes Customer automations start from your events


Data portability Clean export of every record Trust: customers stay because they can leave


Extensibility Custom fields, custom views, room for customer-built screens The workaround lives inside your product


Be the platform Your data and reliability are the base other tools build on Proprietary data and uptime are hard to rebuild


Watch the workarounds Ask customers which spreadsheets they keep next to you Each one is a roadmap item with proof of demand


The categories customers rebuild first are the ones closest to their own process. In Retool's 2026 survey, those were workflow automations, internal admin tools, BI tools, and CRMs and form builders. If your product sits in one of those categories, the defense table above is your roadmap.

## Frequently Asked Questions


Should I build or buy software in 2026?


Buy software for systems of record such as accounting, payroll, and regulated data, where a vendor carries the risk and the workflow is the same in every company. Build the operational tools that are specific to your business, such as a CRM shaped like your pipeline, a client portal, or an operations dashboard. In 2026 you can build those by describing them to an AI app builder, without a development team.


How do I decide between build vs buy software for a small business?


Ask four questions. Is the workflow your edge or the same everywhere? Does a regulator or auditor check it? How many seats would you pay for to use a small part of a product? Who will change the tool when the process changes? If the workflow is yours, unregulated, and changes often, build it. If it is standard, regulated, or costly to get wrong, buy it. Many businesses do both: they keep the system of record and build the missing piece next to it.


Can you build your own CRM with AI?


Yes. An AI app builder such as Taskade Genesis can generate a CRM from a plain-English description of your sales process. The result includes customer records, pipeline views, an AI agent that can help qualify leads, and automations for follow-ups. Before you run a team on it, test it with real data, configure permissions, and check each automation step.


What is the total cost of owning a custom-built business app?


The total cost is more than the price of the builder. Add the hours to describe, test, and adjust the app, the time to keep its data clean and its permissions correct, the integrations it depends on, and the time to fix it when a process or a connected tool changes. Count who owns that work after launch. If nobody does, the app turns back into a spreadsheet workaround. Compare that total with the seats you would pay for, not with the subscription price alone.


Is it cheaper to build software than buy SaaS?


It depends on the tool. A subscription price is easy to compare, but the real cost of a built tool also includes the time to test it, keep data clean, manage permissions, connect integrations, and fix it when something breaks. Building usually wins for a small operational tool that replaces several seats or a daily spreadsheet workaround. Buying usually wins for accounting, regulated workflows, and security-sensitive systems.


What software can non-developers build with AI?


Non-developers commonly build CRMs, client portals, operations dashboards, intake and booking systems, invoice trackers, inventory tools, internal directories, and approval workflow apps. In a first-party census of 471 top-traffic paid Taskade Genesis apps, dashboards and analytics were the largest category at 28.2% of traffic, followed by calculators and tools and by booking and scheduling apps.


What should a business still buy instead of build?


Keep buying payroll, the accounting ledger, tax filing, email delivery at scale, payments processing, and any system that holds regulated data or must pass an audit. These products carry legal and security risk that a vendor is set up to manage. A built tool can still sit next to them, for example an invoice tracker that reads from the accounting system your accountant uses.
